course.title: Unity C# Scripting & Engine Architecture: Advanced Patterns, Systems & Production Code
course.description: An advanced deep-dive into Unity engine architecture for developers who have completed the beginner course. Covers event-driven architecture, ScriptableObject patterns, custom editors, the Job System, DOTS/ECS fundamentals, addressables, advanced optimization, and production-grade code architecture. By the end, you will architect scalable game systems, write editor tools, understand Unity's memory model, and build performance-critical code using modern Unity APIs.

blocks.value: Beyond MonoBehaviour: Clean Architecture
The beginner course taught component-based design. At the intermediate level, you separate concerns further — business logic should not live in MonoBehaviours that are coupled to Unity's lifecycle.
Core principles of clean Unity architecture:

items: **Single Responsibility** — Each class does one thing. A PlayerMovement class should not handle UI or audio.
**Dependency Inversion** — High-level modules depend on abstractions (interfaces), not concrete implementations.
**Composition over Inheritance** — Favor composing behaviors from smaller parts rather than deep inheritance chains.
**Separation of Concerns** — Split game logic, presentation, input, and data into distinct layers.

blocks.value: The Service Locator Pattern
Service Locator is a global registry of services. It is easy to implement but easy to abuse.

items: Easy to implement, easy to abuse
Hides dependencies — you cannot tell what a class needs by looking at its constructor
Hard to test — services are global state
Good for: small projects, rapid prototyping, truly global systems (Audio, Input)

blocks.output: Service Locator: global registry with hidden dependencies. Easy to set up but creates tight coupling to global state.

blocks.question: Why is Service Locator considered an anti-pattern in large projects?
options: It is too slow at runtime
It hides dependencies, making code hard to test and maintain
It requires too many interfaces
It only works with MonoBehaviours
blocks.correctAnswer: It hides dependencies, making code hard to test and maintain
blocks.explanation: Service Locator makes dependencies implicit. You cannot tell what a class needs by looking at its constructor. This makes unit testing impossible (you cannot mock dependencies) and maintenance difficult because changing one service can break classes you did not know used it.

blocks.value: Dependency Injection (DI)
Dependency Injection is the opposite of Service Locator. Dependencies are passed in explicitly, not found globally.

items: Dependencies are explicit — constructor tells you everything the class needs
Easy to mock for unit tests
More setup code, but pays off in large projects
Good for: complex systems, teams, long-term maintenance

blocks.output: Dependency Injection: explicit constructor parameters, factory wiring for MonoBehaviours, and pure C# classes with constructor injection.

blocks.value: DI Container: Manual Wiring
For larger projects, a simple DI container can automate wiring without external libraries like Zenject.

blocks.output: Simple DI Container with singleton registration, factory registration, and a GameBootstrapper that wires everything at startup.

blocks.question: What is the main advantage of Dependency Injection over Service Locator?
options: DI runs faster at runtime
DI makes dependencies explicit and testable
DI requires less code to set up
DI works without MonoBehaviours
blocks.correctAnswer: DI makes dependencies explicit and testable
blocks.explanation: The key advantage of DI is that dependencies are visible in constructors. This makes it obvious what a class needs, enables easy mocking in unit tests, and prevents hidden coupling to global state. Service Locator hides these dependencies.

parts.partTitle: Part 3: Event Bus Pattern — Decoupled Communication

blocks.value: Event Bus Pattern: Decoupled Communication
Direct references between objects create tight coupling. The Event Bus lets objects communicate without knowing about each other.
When to use Event Bus vs direct references:

items: Use **direct references** for parent-child relationships and tightly coupled systems (Player → PlayerHealth)
Use **Event Bus** for cross-cutting concerns (EnemyDied → UI updates, score, achievements, spawn manager)
Use **C# events** on components for local notifications within a subsystem
Use **UnityEvents** (Inspector-configurable) for designer-friendly hooks

blocks.output: Type-safe generic Event Bus with struct events and a publisher that knows nothing about subscribers.

blocks.value: Subscribers: Completely Decoupled

blocks.output: Multiple decoupled subscribers (ScoreManager, AchievementTracker, SpawnManager) responding to the same event without knowing about each other.

blocks.question: Your game has 15 different systems that need to respond when a player completes a level (UI, achievements, analytics, save system, next level unlock). What is the best architecture?
options: Have the LevelManager hold direct references to all 15 systems and call their methods
Use an Event Bus where LevelManager publishes a LevelCompletedEvent and each system subscribes independently
Use a giant switch statement in LevelManager
Have each system poll LevelManager every frame to check if the level is done
blocks.correctAnswer: Use an Event Bus where LevelManager publishes a LevelCompletedEvent and each system subscribes independently
blocks.explanation: Direct references create a maintenance nightmare — add a 16th system and you must modify LevelManager. A switch statement is unmaintainable. Polling wastes CPU. The Event Bus decouples the publisher from subscribers: LevelManager knows nothing about who listens, and new systems can subscribe without touching existing code. This is the core of event-driven architecture.

parts.partTitle: Part 4: State Machines for Complex Behaviors

blocks.value: State Machines for Complex Behaviors
Boolean flags (isAttacking, isStunned, isDead) quickly become unmanageable. A proper state machine enforces valid transitions and encapsulates state-specific logic.
Benefits of state machines:

items: Only valid state transitions are allowed — no accidental 'dead but attacking' bugs
Each state is self-contained — enter, update, exit logic is isolated
Easy to debug — you can log every state transition
Scalable — adding new states does not touch existing ones

blocks.output: Generic StateMachine<T> and State<T> base classes with typed state transitions and lifecycle hooks.

blocks.value: Enemy AI State Machine Implementation

blocks.output: Complete Enemy AI with 6 states, valid transitions, encapsulated per-state logic, and global health check that overrides any state.

blocks.question: What is the primary benefit of using a State Machine over boolean flags for AI behavior?
options: State machines use less memory
State machines enforce valid transitions and prevent impossible state combinations
State machines are easier to serialize to JSON
State machines require less code
blocks.correctAnswer: State machines enforce valid transitions and prevent impossible state combinations
blocks.explanation: Boolean flags allow any combination (e.g., isAttacking AND isDead simultaneously). A state machine enforces that only one state is active at a time and that transitions follow defined rules. This eliminates an entire class of bugs where objects are in logically impossible states.

blocks.value: ScriptableObjects as Game Data

ScriptableObjects are data containers that live in your project, not in scenes. They are the foundation of data-driven design — separating 'what can exist' (data) from 'what currently exists' (runtime instances).
Key advantages over MonoBehaviour data:

items: Shared across scenes — no duplication, no sync issues
Designer-friendly — non-programmers can balance stats via Inspector
Version control friendly — changes are in asset files, not scene files
Cannot be modified at runtime in builds (immutable reference data)
Instantiate with CreateInstance<T>() for runtime-modifiable copies

blocks.output: WeaponData ScriptableObject with identity, combat stats, recoil curves, spread mechanics, audio/visual references, and rarity/economy data.

blocks.value: Enemy Data & Loot Tables

blocks.output: EnemyData with AI behavior and scaling, LootTable with weighted random drops, and ItemData for inventory management.

blocks.question: Why are ScriptableObjects better than storing data in MonoBehaviour components for game balancing?
options: ScriptableObjects run faster at runtime
ScriptableObjects are shared assets editable outside scenes, making version control and balancing easier
ScriptableObjects can only be created by programmers
ScriptableObjects automatically sync data between all scenes
blocks.correctAnswer: ScriptableObjects are shared assets editable outside scenes, making version control and balancing easier
blocks.explanation: ScriptableObjects live as asset files, not in scene files. This means designers can tweak values without opening scenes, changes are tracked in version control as small diffs (not massive scene file changes), and the same data asset can be referenced across multiple scenes without duplication.
